source.title: Mini Habits
source.attribution: A summary of Mini Habits by Stephen Guise (2013). Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.
source.notes: Original summary written by Reborn; contains no text from the book. The book is in copyright.

cards.title: Make the daily goal so small it feels almost silly
cards.body:
Guise's core idea is to set a daily habit so small that you can't reasonably fail: one push-up, one paragraph written, one page read. He came to it after struggling with ambitious fitness plans and trying a single push-up instead, which often led to more.

The tiny target removes the dread of starting. On busy or low days you still meet it, so the habit survives. Over time, the repetition builds the routine that big, intimidating goals often never get the chance to.
cards.apply_it: Pick a habit you keep failing at and set a daily minimum so small you would feel silly skipping it.

quiz.question: Why does Guise make daily habit goals so small?
options: Small goals are the only ones worth having
So you can meet them every day, even on bad days, and the habit takes root
Because big goals are unethical
To avoid ever doing more
quiz.explanation: A target you can't fail keeps the habit alive while the routine forms.

cards.title: Lean on a little willpower, not on motivation
cards.body:
Guise argues that motivation is unreliable: it rises and falls with mood, sleep and stress, so plans built on it collapse on bad days. Willpower can be relied on in small doses, and forcing yourself to do something tiny costs very little of it.

That's why mini habits pair well with willpower. You don't need to feel like doing it; you only need a small push to begin. Waiting to feel inspired before working out or writing often means waiting forever.
cards.apply_it: Next time you think 'I don't feel like it', do the tiny version anyway and notice how much effort it actually took.

quiz.question: Why does Guise prefer willpower over motivation for building habits?
options: Motivation is fickle, while a small push of willpower is dependable
Willpower is unlimited
Motivation is always harmful
He thinks habits shouldn't involve any effort
quiz.explanation: Feelings fluctuate; a tiny demand on willpower can be met almost every day.

cards.title: Do extra when you can, but keep the requirement tiny
cards.body:
Once you start, you will often keep going: one page becomes ten. Guise encourages this extra effort but warns against quietly raising the official target because of it.

The minimum is what protects you on bad days. If you start expecting ten pages, the habit becomes intimidating again and the old resistance returns. Think of everything beyond the minimum as a bonus, welcome but never required. Low expectations combined with frequent overachievement feel good and keep you coming back.
cards.apply_it: Write down your mini habit's minimum and treat anything extra today as a bonus, not the new standard.

quiz.question: What does Guise say you should do after you regularly exceed your mini habit?
options: Raise the minimum immediately
Stop once you hit the minimum
Keep the official requirement small and treat extra work as a bonus
Switch to a different habit
quiz.explanation: Raising the bar brings back resistance; the small minimum keeps the habit safe.

cards.title: Build only a few habits at a time
cards.body:
Even tiny habits add up when you stack too many. Guise recommends working on only a handful at once, so you can reliably meet all of them every day.

It's tempting, especially at New Year or after reading a self-help book, to overhaul your whole life at once. But a long list of new routines spreads your attention thin, and missing several in a day feels like failure. A short list you complete daily builds confidence and leaves room to add more once the first ones become automatic.
cards.apply_it: Look at the habits you're trying to build and cut the list down to the two or three that matter most.

quiz.question: What does Guise recommend about the number of habits to work on?
options: As many as possible, since each one is tiny
Only one per year
Just a few at a time, so you can meet all of them daily
None until you feel motivated
quiz.explanation: A short list you finish every day beats a long list you keep missing.

cards.title: Check off each day so your progress is visible
cards.body:
Guise suggests tracking mini habits in a simple, visible way, such as marking a calendar or ticking a list each day you hit the minimum. The record keeps you honest and makes the habit harder to forget.

Seeing a growing row of completed days also builds quiet satisfaction and helps you notice when the behaviour is becoming automatic, which is when you might consider adding another small habit. A paper calendar, a note on your phone or a habit app all work; the point is that the tracking takes seconds.
cards.apply_it: Set up a simple tracker today, a paper calendar or phone note, and mark it as soon as you complete your mini habit.

quiz.question: What role does daily tracking play in Guise's method?
options: It replaces the need for doing the habit
It keeps you accountable and shows when a habit is becoming automatic
It is only useful for big goals
It should be done once a month
quiz.explanation: A quick daily check-off keeps you on track and reveals your progress.

cards.title: Habits live in a part of the brain that changes slowly
cards.body:
Guise describes two brain systems that matter for habits. One part handles automatic routines; it is efficient but stubborn and doesn't think about long-term consequences. The prefrontal cortex is the planner that can see the bigger picture and override impulses, but it tires easily.

Building a habit means using the planner to train the autopilot, through repetition and reward. Because the automatic part resists sudden change, dramatic overhauls often bounce back. Small, repeated actions work with how this system learns instead of fighting it.
cards.apply_it: Think of a change that didn't last. Was it a sudden overhaul? Write a version small enough to repeat daily.

quiz.question: In Guise's explanation, how does a new habit get formed?
options: By one big burst of effort
By avoiding all rewards
By waiting for the automatic part to change by itself
By the planning part of the brain repeatedly training the automatic part
quiz.explanation: The planner guides the behaviour until repetition and reward make it automatic.

cards.title: Forget the 21-day myth: habits can take months to form
cards.body:
Guise rejects the popular idea that a habit takes 21 or 30 days. He cites a 2009 study in which the time for a behaviour to become automatic averaged around 66 days, with a very wide range of roughly 18 to 254 days depending on the person and the habit.

The practical lesson is not to expect a habit to be locked in by a fixed date, and not to panic if it still takes effort after a month. Keep going until the behaviour feels automatic, however long that takes. Tiny daily habits make a longer timeline far easier to sustain.
cards.apply_it: Look at a habit you started recently. Commit to keeping it up until it feels automatic, not until a set number of days.

quiz.question: What did the study Guise cites find about how long habits take to form?
options: Around 66 days on average, with a wide range between people
Exactly 21 days for everyone
One week at most
Habits never form
quiz.explanation: The average was about 66 days, but some people took far less or far more time.

cards.title: Expect excitement to fade as a habit takes hold
cards.body:
Guise points out an awkward pattern: as a behaviour becomes a habit, the emotion around it fades. The first weeks of a new routine feel exciting; later the same routine feels ordinary. He calls this decreasing enthusiasm.

This is a problem for anyone who relies on feeling motivated, because the motivation drops just as the habit is forming, and many people quit at that point. Guise suggests reading the fading excitement as a sign of progress, not a sign that something is wrong.
cards.apply_it: If a habit has started to feel dull, write down: 'This is a sign it's becoming automatic.' Then do the minimum.

quiz.question: Why does Guise think motivation-based plans often fail just as a habit forms?
options: Because habits get harder over time
Because people get too strong
Because enthusiasm naturally fades as the behaviour becomes routine
Because rewards stop working
quiz.explanation: As behaviour becomes habitual it feels less exciting, so motivation drops.

cards.title: Treat willpower as something you can strengthen with use
cards.body:
Guise presents willpower as more dependable than motivation, and also as something that can be built up over time. Regularly asking a little of yourself, and succeeding, makes it easier to follow through next time, much as regular light training builds a muscle.

Mini habits fit this approach: each one is a small daily rep of self-control. Instead of testing willpower with an enormous demand that is likely to fail, you exercise it with a demand you can always meet, and gradually grow the capacity to do more.
cards.apply_it: Choose one tiny act of self-control to practise daily this week, such as making your bed straight after waking.

quiz.question: How do mini habits relate to willpower, in Guise's view?
options: They use up all your willpower
They work like small daily reps that strengthen willpower over time
They make willpower irrelevant
They only work if you have strong willpower already
quiz.explanation: Small demands you always meet act as training, building your capacity for self-control.

cards.title: Tiny goals keep the effort and dread of a habit low
cards.body:
Guise draws on research about 'ego depletion', the idea that self-control runs down with use. He lists factors linked to it, including effort, how difficult a task seems, negative feelings and tiredness, and argues that mini habits keep each of these to a minimum.

It's worth knowing that later large studies have struggled to replicate the ego depletion effect, and the idea is now debated. Even so, the practical point holds up in daily life: a task that feels effortless and low-stakes is easier to start when you are tired or low.
cards.apply_it: Before a hard task, ask: how can I make this feel less effortful and less daunting? Shrink it until it does.

quiz.question: Which statement about ego depletion fits this card?
options: It is proven beyond doubt
Guise cites it, but later studies have questioned it
Guise rejects it completely
It only applies to athletes
quiz.explanation: Guise uses the research, but large replication attempts have since cast doubt on it.

cards.title: Step just outside your comfort zone, not miles beyond it
cards.body:
Guise pictures your comfort zone as a boundary. A huge leap far outside it, like going from no exercise to an hour a day, triggers strong inner pushback, and you snap back to old ways.

Mini habits take you only just past the edge. The step is small enough that your mind doesn't raise alarms, yet it still counts as growth. Repeated daily, these small steps gradually push the boundary outwards, so what once felt like a stretch becomes normal. Change through steady expansion is gentler and more likely to last than one dramatic jump.
cards.apply_it: Pick a goal that feels intimidating. Write the smallest step that is just a little outside your comfort zone.

quiz.question: How do mini habits expand your comfort zone, according to Guise?
options: By forcing a dramatic leap
By changing your environment entirely
By avoiding any discomfort
By taking small steps just past its edge, repeated daily
quiz.explanation: Tiny steps beyond the boundary avoid pushback and gradually stretch it outwards.

cards.title: Small habits slip past resistance that big plans trigger
cards.body:
Guise describes mini habits as a kind of Trojan horse. A large goal announces itself and your mind braces against it; a tiny one seems too harmless to fight. Once you are in motion, it is easier to continue.

He notes that resistance shows up at two points: before you start, and while you are doing the task. A tiny goal deals with both, because the start is easy and the finish line is close. That lets a small new behaviour gradually compete with strong, long-established habits that would otherwise crowd it out.
cards.apply_it: Notice when you feel resistance to a task today. Shrink the task until the resistance goes quiet, then start.

quiz.question: Why does Guise compare mini habits to a Trojan horse?
options: They look too small to resist, so they get past your inner defences
They are secretly huge goals
They are only for soldiers
They trick other people
quiz.explanation: Tiny goals don't trigger the pushback that big ones do, so you start more easily.

cards.title: Mini habits build good behaviours; serious addictions need other help
cards.body:
Guise is clear about what his method is for. Mini habits are a way of adding positive behaviours, such as reading, exercise or writing. They can help crowd out passive bad habits like procrastination or idleness, because your time and energy go somewhere useful.

But he does not present them as a way to quit active addictions, such as heavy drinking. Those involve strong cravings and often need other strategies and support. Being honest about a tool's limits helps you use it well and seek the right help where it's needed.
cards.apply_it: Sort the changes you want into 'add something good' and 'stop something harmful'. Use mini habits for the first list.

quiz.question: What does Guise say mini habits are NOT designed for?
options: Starting to read more
Exercising regularly
Quitting active addictions such as heavy drinking
Writing every day
quiz.explanation: Mini habits add positive behaviours; strong addictions need other approaches and support.

cards.title: Test-drive a mini habit for a week before committing
cards.body:
Guise suggests that before settling on a long-term plan, you try a mini habit for a week. The trial shows you whether the habit is truly small enough, whether it fits your day, and how it feels to do it consistently.

After the trial you can decide whether to focus on a single habit or run a few together. Treating the first week as an experiment takes the pressure off getting everything right at once, and gives you real information instead of guesses about what will work.
cards.apply_it: Pick one mini habit and run a seven-day trial. At the end, note what was easy, what was awkward and what you'd change.

quiz.question: Why does Guise recommend a one-week trial?
options: To prove you can do something hard
Because habits form in a week
To earn a reward
To learn whether the habit fits your life before committing long term
quiz.explanation: A short trial gives you real feedback on whether the habit is small enough and workable.

cards.title: Ask 'why' repeatedly to check a habit really matters to you
cards.body:
Guise recommends what he calls the Why Drill. For each habit you want, ask why you want it, then ask why again about your answer, and keep going until you reach a core reason.

Sometimes this reveals a deep value, like health to enjoy time with your children. Sometimes it shows the habit came from outside pressure or comparison rather than something you care about. Habits rooted in your own values are worth the effort; those borrowed from others are easier to drop. The drill helps you choose well before you start.
cards.apply_it: Pick one habit and ask yourself 'why?' five times in a row, writing each answer. What's at the bottom?

quiz.question: What is the goal of Guise's Why Drill?
options: To uncover whether a habit connects to your own core values
To find excuses not to start
To impress other people
To pick as many habits as possible
quiz.explanation: Repeated 'why' questions reveal whether a habit is truly yours or borrowed from others.

cards.title: Pick a cue that suits you: a time, an activity, or 'before bed'
cards.body:
Guise describes two main kinds of habit cue. A time-based cue ties the habit to a clock time, such as 7am. An activity-based cue ties it to something you already do, such as after brushing your teeth.

He also allows a looser option: doing the mini habit any time before you go to bed. If a strict cue keeps causing stress or missed days, a general daily deadline can work better, because the habit is so small you can fit it in almost anywhere. Choose the cue that helps you remember without becoming a burden.
cards.apply_it: Decide the cue for your mini habit: a set time, after an existing activity, or simply 'before bed'. Write it down.

quiz.question: What does Guise suggest if a specific cue keeps causing stress or missed days?
options: Give up the habit
Do the habit three times a day
Use a general cue, such as any time before bed
Add a punishment
quiz.explanation: A flexible daily deadline can work because the habit is small enough to fit anywhere.

cards.title: Reward yourself often, especially in the early days
cards.body:
Many good habits, like reading or exercise, take a long time to show their full benefits. Guise suggests filling that gap with your own rewards: something small and pleasant after you complete your mini habit, such as a short rest, a favourite song or a treat you enjoy.

Rewards strengthen the link between the action and a good feeling, which helps the habit stick. Over time, he notes, the habit itself can start to feel rewarding. Make sure the reward doesn't work against the habit, such as a large dessert after a workout.
cards.apply_it: Choose a small, healthy reward for your mini habit and give it to yourself every time you do it this week.

quiz.question: Why does Guise recommend rewarding mini habits?
options: Rewards are the main goal of habits
Many habits pay off slowly, and rewards strengthen the habit meanwhile
Rewards replace the need to do the habit
Only big rewards work
quiz.explanation: Small rewards bridge the gap until the habit's own benefits show up.

cards.title: Be glad about every bit of progress, however small
cards.body:
One of Guise's rules is to be happy with all progress. A single page read or one minute of exercise is still a step forward compared with doing nothing.

This matters because self-criticism makes habits feel heavy and unpleasant, and people avoid what feels unpleasant. Celebrating small steps does the opposite: it makes you more willing to return tomorrow. It's not about lowering standards forever, but about recognising that consistent small gains add up and deserve credit along the way.
cards.apply_it: At the end of today, write one small thing you did towards a goal and acknowledge it, however minor it seems.

quiz.question: Why does Guise say you should be happy with all progress?
options: So you never have to do more
Because criticism makes habits unpleasant, while celebrating small steps keeps you coming back
Because small steps are better than big ones
To impress others
quiz.explanation: Positive feelings about small steps make you more likely to repeat them.

cards.title: Stay level-headed; a boring habit is a winning habit
cards.body:
Guise warns against getting carried away when a new habit goes well, and against feeling let down when the excitement fades. He suggests a calm, steady attitude instead.

When a habit starts to feel boring, that is often a sign of success: the behaviour is turning automatic and no longer needs emotional fuel. People who expect constant excitement tend to quit at exactly this stage. Steady repetition without drama is what a formed habit looks like.
cards.apply_it: If a habit feels flat this week, keep doing it calmly. Remind yourself that routine is the goal.

quiz.question: How does Guise interpret a habit starting to feel boring?
options: As a sign to quit
As a sign you need a bigger goal
As a sign you chose the wrong habit
As a sign it is becoming automatic
quiz.explanation: Boredom often means the behaviour no longer needs emotion to happen; it's turning into a habit.

cards.title: Know the signs that a habit has fully formed
cards.body:
Guise lists signals that a mini habit has become a true habit. You feel little or no resistance before doing it. You do it without deciding to, almost on autopilot. It no longer feels like a big deal emotionally. And you may start seeing yourself differently, for example as someone who writes or exercises.

These signs help you decide when to add another habit. He advises against rushing: until the signs appear, keep the habit small and keep repeating it. Moving on too early can leave a half-formed habit to fade.
cards.apply_it: Check your current habit against these signs: no resistance, no decision needed, no big emotion. How many apply?

quiz.question: Which is a sign, according to Guise, that a habit has formed?
options: You do it without needing to decide or push yourself
You feel strong excitement every time
You need more rewards
You think about it constantly
quiz.explanation: A formed habit happens with little resistance or deliberation.

cards.title: When resistance is strong, make the step even smaller
cards.body:
Even a mini habit can sometimes feel hard: a bad day, a busy week, or a goal that wasn't small enough after all. Guise's rule is simple: if you notice strong resistance, back off and shrink the step further.

For example, if one healthy meal feels like too much, start with one bite of fruit. The aim is to keep the chain of action going, not to prove toughness. A tiny step taken is worth far more to the habit than a bigger step that never happens.
cards.apply_it: If you're avoiding a habit right now, cut it in half, then in half again, and do that version today.

quiz.question: What does Guise advise when you feel strong resistance to a mini habit?
options: Push through with maximum effort
Skip it for a week
Back off and make the step even smaller
Add another habit to balance it
quiz.explanation: Shrinking the step keeps you acting, which is what builds the habit.

cards.title: Remind yourself how easy the task really is
cards.body:
Guise notes that we tend to build up tasks in our heads until they feel heavier than they are. A big willpower battle with yourself is one you usually lose.

His advice is to remind yourself just how easy your mini habit is. 'It's only one push-up' or 'just fifty words' takes the drama out. Framing the task honestly as small avoids the inner struggle altogether, so you can simply start. Ease, not toughness, is what makes daily consistency possible.
cards.apply_it: Next time you hesitate, say out loud what the task actually is, e.g. 'It's only one page.' Then do it.

quiz.question: Why does Guise suggest reminding yourself how easy the habit is?
options: To make you feel lazy
To trick other people
To prove the habit is pointless
To avoid a draining willpower battle and simply begin
quiz.explanation: Seeing the task as small removes the inner struggle that blocks starting.

cards.title: No step is too small to be worth taking
cards.body:
Guise insists you should never dismiss a step as too small to count. It can feel silly to celebrate one push-up or one sentence, especially when you compare yourself with people doing far more.

But he argues that small, repeated steps fit how the brain forms new patterns: it learns from repetition rather than from occasional large efforts. The size of each step matters less than the fact that it happens every day. Dismissing small steps is often the thought that stops people from starting at all.
cards.apply_it: Notice any thought today like 'that's too small to matter'. Do the small thing anyway and count it.

quiz.question: Why does Guise say no step is too small?
options: The brain forms patterns through repetition, which tiny steps provide
Small steps are always enjoyable
Big steps are dangerous
Small steps are faster to finish
quiz.explanation: Repetition, not size, is what builds new patterns in the brain.

cards.title: Daily small wins rebuild belief in your own follow-through
cards.body:
Guise highlights self-efficacy: your belief that you can do what you set out to do. Repeated failure with ambitious goals erodes it, and some people start to feel nothing they try will work.

Mini habits reverse this. Because the daily target is almost impossible to miss, you succeed every day, and each success is evidence that you can keep your word to yourself. That growing confidence makes it easier to take on more challenging goals later.
cards.apply_it: Set one tiny promise to yourself for today and keep it. Note how it feels to follow through.

quiz.question: How do mini habits affect self-efficacy, according to Guise?
options: They lower it by setting easy goals
They have no effect
They build it, because daily success shows you can follow through
They only help people who are already confident
quiz.explanation: Consistent daily wins provide proof that you can keep commitments to yourself.

cards.title: Choosing to do more feels better than being forced to
cards.body:
Guise argues that people resist being controlled, even by their own rigid plans. A demanding schedule can feel like an order, and part of you rebels against it.

With a mini habit, the requirement is tiny and everything beyond it is your own choice. When you decide to read another chapter, it feels like freedom, not obligation. Keeping that sense of autonomy makes the habit something you want to do, which helps you keep it up over the long term.
cards.apply_it: After your minimum today, pause and ask: do I want to do more? Let the answer be a genuine choice.

quiz.question: Why does Guise think autonomy helps mini habits work?
options: Because rules are always bad
Because extra effort feels like a free choice rather than an order you resist
Because autonomy means skipping the habit
Because other people decide for you
quiz.explanation: Freely chosen effort avoids the inner rebellion that strict demands can trigger.

cards.title: Turn a vague goal into one concrete action you can do every day
cards.body:
Big goals like 'get fit' or 'be a writer' are abstract; you can't do them today. Guise points out that mini habits connect these goals to a specific daily action, such as one push-up or a few sentences, that you can do regardless of mood.

This closes the gap between wanting and doing. Instead of waiting for the right moment to work on a big dream, you touch it every single day. Over months, these concrete actions slowly build the result that the abstract goal described.
cards.apply_it: Write one big goal at the top of a page. Underneath, write the smallest concrete action toward it you could do daily.

quiz.question: What do mini habits do for big abstract goals, in Guise's view?
options: Replace them with small goals forever
Link them to a specific action you can do daily, whatever your mood
Make them unnecessary
Delay them until you're ready
quiz.explanation: A tiny daily action gives a vague goal a concrete, regular foothold.

cards.title: If change keeps failing, question the strategy before yourself
cards.body:
Guise starts from a hopeful claim: when people repeatedly fail to change, the problem is often the method, not their character. Plans that depend on high motivation or big daily targets set most people up to fail, and the failures then get blamed on laziness or weakness.

He experienced this himself with years of on-and-off exercise. Switching to a smaller approach worked where self-criticism and pep talks did not. If a plan has failed you many times, change the plan before concluding that you're the problem.
cards.apply_it: Think of a change you've tried many times. Write down what the strategy was, and one way to make it much smaller.

quiz.question: What does Guise say about repeated failure to build habits?
options: It proves a person lacks discipline
It is caused by bad luck
It means you should stop trying
It often points to a poor strategy rather than a personal flaw
quiz.explanation: Many common methods rely on motivation and big targets; the method may be what fails.

cards.title: Much of what you do each day runs on habit
cards.body:
Guise cites research from Duke University suggesting that roughly 45% of our everyday behaviour is habitual, done in similar ways and contexts without much thought.

If a large share of your day runs on autopilot, then the quality of your habits shapes the quality of your life far more than occasional bursts of effort do. That's the case for investing in habits: once a good behaviour becomes automatic, it keeps paying off without demanding fresh willpower every day.
cards.apply_it: Look at the first two hours of your day. Which actions happen on autopilot? Pick one to improve.

quiz.question: What point does Guise make by citing research that much behaviour is habitual?
options: Since so much of life runs on autopilot, improving habits has a big effect
Habits don't matter much
People should avoid all habits
Willpower controls most of what we do
quiz.explanation: If a large share of behaviour is automatic, good habits shape daily life significantly.

cards.title: A tiny habit can grow naturally into a bigger routine
cards.body:
Guise kept his one push-up habit going for months. By then exercise had become part of his life, and moving on to regular gym sessions felt like a natural next step rather than a struggle.

The point is that mini habits are not a ceiling. They lay the groundwork, building routine and confidence, so that bigger steps become easier later. Instead of forcing a big routine at the start, let the small one take root first and grow from there when it feels easy to do so.
cards.apply_it: Look at a mini habit you've kept for a while. Is there a natural next step that now feels easy rather than forced?

quiz.question: What happened when Guise had kept his tiny exercise habit for months?
options: He quit exercising
He raised his minimum to 100 push-ups
Moving to regular gym sessions felt like a natural, easy step
He switched to a reading habit instead
quiz.explanation: The tiny habit built a foundation that made a bigger routine feel easy.
